questions.q: What is cryptography, at its simplest definition?
options: The science of protecting information so that only the right people can read or verify it
A specific type of cryptocurrency
The process of mining new blocks
A programming language used for smart contracts
questions.explain: Like locking a message in a box only the right person has the key to, cryptography protects information from anyone who shouldn't be able to read or verify it.

questions.q: What three things does cryptography actually solve for, specifically for blockchain?
options: Trust, security, and verification
Speed, storage, and cost
Marketing, branding, and design
Taxes, legal compliance, and licensing
questions.explain: Cryptography's real job in blockchain is making trustless systems possible — ones where the math itself guarantees the rules are followed.

questions.q: What does a "trustless system" actually mean?
options: A system where participants don't need to personally trust each other, because the math enforces the rules
A system where nobody can be trusted at all, including the developers
A system with no security whatsoever
A system that requires a bank to operate
questions.explain: Trustless doesn't mean untrustworthy — it means trust is built into the mathematics and cryptography itself, not into any single person or institution.

questions.q: Which of these is a real, everyday example of cryptography already at work, mentioned in this lesson?
options: End-to-end encrypted messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal
Only Bitcoin transactions
Physical door locks
Paper checks
questions.explain: End-to-end encryption in apps like WhatsApp and Signal ensures only the sender and recipient can actually read a message — a real, everyday cryptography use case.

questions.q: According to this lesson's roadmap, what comes right after symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption?
options: Public and private keys, then digital signatures
Mining and consensus algorithms
Writing your first smart contract
Setting up a Solidity development environment
questions.explain: This chapter builds from hash functions, to symmetric/asymmetric encryption, to public/private keys, and finally to digital signatures in Lesson 3.
